Field surveys of Pacora (Plagioscion surinamensis) from the Amazon basin indicate that females attain a total length at puberty of 27.3 centimeters [Lp = 27.3 centimeters], marking the onset of gonadal maturation in this large-bodied sciaenid. This length corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 262 grams [Wwp = 262 grams], derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship, and represents a considerable investment in somatic growth prior to reproductive activation. The protracted juvenile phase leading to this milestone is energetically intensive, as individuals must accumulate sufficient reserves to support future spawning events. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the length at first maturity in Plagioscion surinamensis is consistent with a life-history strategy emphasizing delayed reproduction in favor of achieving a larger body size. The ecological implications of this pattern are evident in the species' seasonal migrations along flooded forests, where mature individuals seek out suitable spawning grounds. Gonadal recrudescence in females is closely tied to the rising water levels of the rainy season, ensuring that newly hatched larvae encounter favorable conditions for growth and survival.

At the upper end of the size spectrum, the ultimate total length recorded for Plagioscion surinamensis reaches 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], characterizing this species as one of the larger members of the Sciaenidae in neotropical freshwaters. This maximal length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 4700 grams [Wwi = 4700 grams], reflecting the substantial biomass accumulation possible in productive floodplain habitats. Such asymptotic dimensions are attained over a prolonged lifespan; available evidence from mark-recapture studies and otolith microchemistry suggests that individuals can live for approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This longevity is comparable to that reported for the closely related species Plagioscion squamosissimus, indicating a conservative life-history strategy within the genus. The combination of large body size and extended lifespan likely confers a reproductive advantage, as older, larger females produce disproportionately more offspring. Adult individuals are frequently captured in gillnet surveys at depths exceeding ten meters, demonstrating their occupation of deeper channel habitats during the dry season.

In terms of early life history, the yolk-sac larva of Pacora emerges from the egg after an incubation period of approximately 5.5 days [ab = approximately 5.5 days] when water temperatures are maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The hatchling wet weight at birth is 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams], a minute mass derived from an egg diameter of roughly one millimeter. This brief embryonic phase is typical of warm-water teleosts, where elevated metabolic rates accelerate developmental processes. During the subsequent lecithotrophic stage, the prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for nourishment, displaying a characteristic non-feeding behavior as its mouthparts and digestive system continue to differentiate. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs as the yolk sac is resorbed, typically coinciding with the onset of swim bladder inflation. The rapidity of this early development is an adaptation to the highly seasonal and productive floodplain environment, where planktonic food resources become abundant following the initial pulse of the rainy season. Mortality during this vulnerable larval window is exceptionally high, driven by predation and fluctuating oxygen levels.

The maximum reproductive output of Plagioscion surinamensis has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions. At a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], mature females produce approximately 1370 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1370 eggs per spawning event] during the peak spawning period, maintained over several consecutive days. This per-event fecundity, combined with a spawning frequency of roughly one event per year [F_R_i = roughly one event per year], yields a substantial annual reproductive effort. The oocytes are small and pelagic, with a diameter of about one millimeter, facilitating their dispersal by river currents. Batch spawning is the predominant mode of reproduction, allowing females to spread their reproductive investment across multiple events within a single season. The high fecundity compensates for the elevated mortality experienced during the early pelagic larval phase, which is typical of many sciaenids inhabiting dynamic riverine systems. Observations of gravid individuals in the field suggest that spawning is synchronized with rising water levels, maximizing the availability of inundated floodplain nursery areas.

Comparisons of growth parameters between sexes reveal that female Plagioscion surinamensis achieve a larger adult body size than males, a pattern common among sciaenid fishes. The species' trophic position as a piscivore and crustacean feeder supports a high energetic demand that fuels the considerable biomass gain needed to transition from a juvenile body mass of 262 grams [Wwp = 262 grams] at puberty to the maximal adult mass of 4700 grams [Wwi = 4700 grams] observed in older females. Achieving this near-seventeen-fold increase in mass requires sustained access to productive floodplain habitats during the annual inundation cycle. The iteroparous reproductive strategy, wherein individuals spawn annually over a lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], allows females to recoup the high energetic costs of gonad development multiple times across their lives. Stable isotope analyses from the lower Amazon indicate that Plagioscion surinamensis occupies a relatively high trophic level within its food web. Ongoing habitat degradation from dam construction and deforestation poses a significant threat to the floodplain spawning grounds essential for larval recruitment.
